intro: Every country faces the same two questions. When people get sick or hurt, who pays for their care? And how can doctors and nurses understand patients who speak different languages and hold different beliefs about health? Nations answer these questions in very different ways, and the answers shape millions of lives.

In this unit you will compare the main ways countries pay for care, from Britain's National Health Service to Germany's sickness funds, Canada's public insurance and the mixed system of the United States. Then you will step into the exam room, where language, family, belief and trust can matter as much as any medicine.

By the end, you will be able to explain each model's strengths and the criticisms made of it, read data on costs and outcomes with care, and describe how listening, interpreters and cultural humility help people from every background get good care.
bigQuestion: What makes a health system fair and effective for everyone it serves?

timeline.t: Germany passes Bismarck's health insurance law for many workers
William Beveridge's report calls for a national health service in Britain
Britain opens the NHS; the UN adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Japan reaches health insurance for nearly everyone
Saskatchewan begins public payment for doctor care in Canada
U.S. Civil Rights Act; Title VI later guides language help in care
President Johnson signs Medicare and Medicaid into law
The Tuskegee syphilis study is exposed and ended
Taiwan starts its National Health Insurance
Anne Fadiman publishes The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down
The Affordable Care Act becomes law in the United States

words.d: a system where the government pays for care with taxes and often owns hospitals
a system where required insurance, paid by workers and employers, covers care
a setup in which one public body pays nearly all medical bills
a system where patients pay for care directly with their own money
the goal that everyone can get needed care without money trouble
the regular payment that buys an insurance plan
a federal-state program that covers many people with low incomes
a choice where gaining one thing means giving up some of another
a person's own understanding of what an illness is and what caused it
a trained person who turns words from one language into another accurately during care
a gap in health or health care between groups of people
a lifelong habit of curiosity and learning from each patient

test.q: Britain's NHS, opened in 1948, is the best-known example of which model?
test.why: The NHS is paid mainly by taxes, the mark of the Beveridge model.

test.q: In the Bismarck model, where does most of the money come from?
test.why: Workers and employers pay shares of paychecks into insurance funds.

test.q: Which country uses national health insurance, where one public plan pays mostly independent doctors?
test.why: Canada's provinces run public plans that pay independent doctors.

test.q: Which program covers most Americans 65 and older?
test.why: Medicare, created in 1965, covers people 65 and older.

test.q: What did the ACA do about preexisting conditions?
choices: Barred insurers from refusing people for them
Required people to pay more for them
test.why: The ACA stopped insurers from turning people away for a preexisting condition.

test.q: According to the OECD, how does U.S. health spending compare with other wealthy countries?
test.why: The U.S. spends about 17 percent of GDP, more than other wealthy countries.

choices: Costs so high a family gives up basic needs
test.why: The WHO uses the term for costs that force families to cut food or housing.

test.q: Which is a fair statement about comparing health systems?
choices: Life expectancy proves which is best
Wait times are the only measure
Every system has trade-offs people weigh differently
Wealthy countries all use one model
test.why: Systems trade off cost, coverage, waits and choice, and values differ.

choices: What do you think caused your illness?
test.why: Kleinman's questions ask about the patient's own view of the illness.

test.q: Why is a trained interpreter usually better than a family member?
choices: Family members cannot speak two languages
Interpreters know medical terms and repeat everything accurately
test.why: Trained interpreters are accurate, private and know medical words.

choices: The doctor repeats the plan twice
The patient explains the plan in their own words
test.why: Teach-back checks the clinician's explanation by having the patient say it back.

test.q: What lesson does Fadiman's book about Lia Lee teach?
choices: Misunderstanding can harm care even when everyone means well
Families should not take part in care
test.why: Fadiman showed both the family and doctors cared, but misunderstanding hurt Lia's care.

test.q: What should a patient do about herbs or supplements they use?
choices: Tell a doctor, nurse or pharmacist
test.why: Some herbs change how medicines work, so clinicians need to know.

test.q: What protection grew stronger after the Tuskegee syphilis study?
test.why: The study led to stronger rules for research, including informed consent.

test.q: Which is an example of a social determinant of health?
test.why: Food, housing, income and safety are conditions that shape health.

write.prompt: Which health system model from this unit do you think best balances cost, coverage and choice? Make a claim, support it with two or three facts or sources from the unit, and explain one criticism of your choice fairly.
tips: Name the model and a country that uses it
Cite at least two facts, such as OECD spending data or Census coverage numbers
Describe one real criticism of your choice and answer it
Use unit terms such as trade-off, coverage and single-payer
